Ender's Game is a pretty famous scifi work, IMO, but the "Ender Trilogy" of sequels (Speaker for the Dead, Xenocide, and Children of the Mind) are all VASTLY superior to both Ender's Game and the "Shadow" sequels.

The Ender books were much more adult in nature, with the now older Ender mentally dealing with what he had done as well as how the colonists interpret the native population's culture/biology. Contrast that with the "Shadow" series where you have the now unneeded battle school children being fought over as commodities on Earth. It's much more action oriented, but overall i found it pretty boring.

Thoughts?
I enjoyed Enders game but Speaker for the dead somehow bored me and I never finished it. I'm not that sold on Card's writing style.
I just started reading Ender's game. It' been on my wishlist for quite some time.

Wow! I've heard the complete opposite from a lot of people! I know a few who really like the Bean half of the sequels.

I haven't gotten around to reading them yet >.> but I really liked Ender's Game, read it years ago.

I couldn't stand the three sequels. It was a huge departure from all of the things that made Ender's Game great. Finally, at the end of Children of the Mind, when there was the possibility of something interesting, the book ended and there was no follow up. The Shadow series, however, returned to all of the things that made Ender's Game great.
This is pretty much how I see it. I still enjoyed the three Game sequels, but nowhere near as much as I did the Shadows or Ender's Game itself.

In early high school I sprinted through Ender's Game, and loved the heck out of it. It was my favorite book. I tried the sequels (Speaker) but it was too different. To slow. No battle school.. So I loved the Shadow series for its action and political intrigue. Definitely not sci-fi, though.

Picking up Speaker again in college, oh man. I think I did all 3 sequels on one summer break. Definitely a different type of book than Ender, but still great.

That emotional eulogy in Speaker was amazing.

I have a fond nostalgia of how much I loved Bean and his story and am tempted to pick up the series where it left off, but Card's writing has gotten so bland lately, I can't do it.

The rest of the Ender Trilogy is on my to-do list; I really enjoyed Ender in Exile and thought that Ender's Shadow was pretty neat as well- the early books in the series are quite different from the others. It goes from a story about training and managing a team to interplanetary exploration!

I love this series. In the audiobook version of Speaker of the Dead, Card explains that his original plan was to write Speaker. However, he couldn't make it work so he instead wrote Ender's Game first, to prepare for Speaker. It took me a while to get into Speaker, but after the first few chapters I fell in love with it too.

The Ender Trilogy sequels was philosophically interesting. Sci-fi authors often walk the range from philosophy to action, finding at some point their own blend of the two, and I feel that Orson Scott Card found his own comfort zone pretty far into philosophy realm, even though the books that made his name were more on the action/intrigue part of that spectrum. I can't blame the man, since he has a great mind and did everything spectacularly well, be it philosophy or intrigue.

You may like to read Zendell's "Requiem for Homo Sapiens", from what I gather. It's so far on the philosophy side of science fiction that I dub this genre "science-philosophy" now.

I disagree. I think that any time OSC tries to delve into more strictly philosophical realms he does it fairly awkwardly. There were still points in the books that were very well written and I still enjoyed the books, but I didn't enjoy them nearly as much as I did Ender's Game or the Shadow series. Sure there's a lot more action in them than philosophy, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Granted I last read through all of these years ago, so take all of this with a grain of salt.

I have no idea why people like Ender's Game. It's a book made up of Mary Sues, it has various homophobic scenes, the author is not intelligent enough to portray intelligent characters except in the hamfisted way of making them magically talented or gifted. The sole philosophical points don't actually pose interesting questions, nor resolve them. It's nowhere near the level of Asimov, or Neal Stephenson.

Really, the book read to me like a pointless and non-interesting rendition of Starship Troopers (regardless of which came first). I say this to ideally give you an explanation for why I dislike the book, and why I can't fathom how other people enjoy it. Hopefully somebody will respond by explaining their interest in this, versus some other superior book with an actual philosophical or satirical narrative.
